claim: The delta-protocadherins (δ-Pcdhs) are a nine-member subfamily of the cadherin superfamily.
source: The delta-protocadherins (δ-Pcdhs) are a nine-member subfamily of the cadherin superfamily (Hulpiau and van Roy, 2009; Nollet et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature establishing the classification and size of the δ-Pcdh subfamily

claim: Individual δ-Pcdhs are important for neural development, including hindbrain formation, axon guidance, and synaptogenesis.
source: Mutagenesis studies have shown that individual δ-Pcdhs are important for neural development, including hindbrain formation, axon guidance, and synaptogenesis (Cooper et al., 2015; Emond et al., 2009; Hayashi et al., 2014; Hoshina et al., 2013; Leung et al., 2013; Light and Jontes, 2017; Uemura et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to mutagenesis studies demonstrating roles in various aspects of neural development

claim: Mutations in PCDH19 are the causative basis of one form of epilepsy in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in PCDH19 are the causative basis of one form of epilepsy (Dibbens et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research establishing the genetic basis of this epilepsy form

claim: Other δ-Pcdhs are implicated in various neurological disorders.
source: other δ-Pcdhs are implicated in various neurological disorders (Chang et al., 2018; Consortium on Complex Epilepsies, 2014; Morrow et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking δ-Pcdhs to neurological disorders

claim: The δ-Pcdh subfamily has been divided into the δ−1 (Pcdh1, Pcdh7, Pcdh9, and Pcdh11x) and δ−2 (Pcdh8, Pcdh10, Pcdh17, Pcdh18, and Pcdh19) subfamilies based on differences in the number of extracellular domains and within the intracellular domain.
source: The δ-Pcdh subfamily has been further divided into the δ−1 (Pcdh1, Pcdh7, Pcdh9, and Pcdh11x) and δ−2 (Pcdh8, Pcdh10, Pcdh17, Pcdh18, and Pcdh19) subfamilies based on differences in the number of extracellular domains and also within the intracellular domain (Redies et al., 2005; Vanhalst et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior classification studies based on structural differences

claim: Double label RNA in situ hybridization studies indicate individual neurons express more than one δ-Pcdh.
source: Double label RNA in situ hybridization studies indicate individual neurons express more than one δ-Pcdh (Etzrodt et al., 2009; Krishna-K et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior expression studies demonstrating co-expression

claim: Mutations in PCDH19 affected cell sorting in both in vitro aggregation assays and in brains of mice.
source: Pederick et al. demonstrated that mutations in PCDH19, a δ−2 family member, affected cell sorting in both in vitro aggregation assays and in brains of mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to a prior study demonstrating effects of PCDH19 mutations on cell sorting

claim: Humans with PCDH19-GCE exhibit abnormal cortical folding patterns.
source: Furthermore, they also showed that humans with PCDH19-GCE exhibit abnormal cortical folding patterns (Pederick et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study demonstrating cortical folding abnormalities in PCDH19-GCE patients

claim: All detectable δ-Pcdhs were expressed in a punctate pattern in the olfactory epithelium, indicating differential expression among OSNs.
source: All detectable δ-Pcdhs were expressed in a punctate pattern, indicating differential expression among OSNs.
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data showing punctate expression patterns

claim: Pcdh1 is more highly expressed in the lateral epithelium, and more weakly medially.
source: For example, Pcdh1 is more highly expressed in the lateral epithelium, and more weakly medially (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data and referenced figures showing regional expression patterns

claim: Pcdh9 and Pcdh17 show the opposite pattern to Pcdh1, and are more strongly expressed medially with relatively low expression laterally.
source: In contrast, other δ-Pcdhs, such as Pcdh9 and Pcdh17, show the opposite pattern, and are more strongly expressed medially with relatively low expression laterally (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data and referenced figures showing regional expression patterns

claim: Pcdh10 expression is dependent upon odorant-mediated activity.
source: One exception was Pcdh10, whose expression we previously demonstrated to be dependent upon odorant-mediated activity (Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study demonstrating activity-dependent expression of Pcdh10

claim: 5–35% of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) co-express any two δ-Pcdhs.
source: We systematically assayed all expressed pairs to show that 5–35% of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) co-express any two δ-Pcdhs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by double label RNA in situ hybridization data quantified and shown in referenced figure

claim: Pcdh1 and Pcdh7 were only co-expressed 8% of the time.
source: For example, Pcdh1 and Pcdh7 were only co-expressed 8% of the time
evidence: Supported by double label RNA in situ hybridization data

claim: Pcdh8 and Pcdh9 were co-expressed 35% of the time.
source: while Pcdh8 and Pcdh9 were co-expressed 35% of the time.
evidence: Supported by double label RNA in situ hybridization data

claim: OSNs expressing the same odorant receptor project to common targets within the olfactory bulb.
source: OSNs expressing the same odorant receptor project to common targets within the olfactory bulb (Ressler et al., 1994; Vassar et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies establishing OSN projection patterns

claim: Mutant analysis of members of the δ-Pcdh and cPcdh subfamilies has shown these genes are important for OSN targeting.
source: Mutant analysis of members of the δ-Pcdh and cPcdh subfamilies has previously shown these genes are important for OSN targeting (Hasegawa et al., 2008; Mountoufaris et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior mutant studies demonstrating roles in OSN targeting

claim: Different OSN populations varied in the proportion of δ-Pcdhs they expressed.
source: Confocal analysis showed all five OSN populations surveyed express varying proportions of different δ-Pcdhs (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by double label RNA in situ hybridization data showing variable co-expression patterns

claim: Pcdh9 was expressed by more than half of all OSNs expressing Olfr558.
source: For example, Pcdh9 was expressed by more than half of all OSNs expressing Olfr558.
evidence: Supported by double label RNA in situ hybridization data quantifying co-expression

claim: ~12% of Olfr557 OSNs expressed Pcdh9.
source: In contrast, ~12% of Olfr557 OSNs expressed Pcdh9.
evidence: Supported by double label RNA in situ hybridization data quantifying co-expression

claim: Individual OSNs expressed anywhere from zero to seven δ-Pcdhs.
source: This revealed that individual OSNs expressed anywhere from zero to seven δ-Pcdhs (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by NanoString single cell RNA analysis data shown in referenced figure

claim: K562 cells do not express endogenous cadherins and are non-adherent.
source: K562 cells are commonly used to study adhesion mediated by cadherins because it is believed they do not express endogenous cadherins and are non-adherent (Ozawa and Kemler, 1998; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies establishing K562 cell properties

claim: The ECTM domain was sufficient to drive homophilic adhesion.
source: Importantly, the ECTM domain was sufficient to drive homophilic adhesion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by aggregation assay data shown in referenced figure

claim: The exogenously expressed protocadherins localized to sites of intracellular contact.
source: As expected, the exogenously expressed protocadherins localized to sites of intracellular contact (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in referenced figure

claim: δ-Pcdh adhesion is highly sensitive to EDTA.
source: We also confirmed that δ-Pcdh adhesion is highly sensitive to EDTA, consistent with being members of the calcium dependent cadherin superfamily (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by aggregation assay data with EDTA treatment shown in referenced figure, and consistent with known cadherin properties

claim: All expressed δ-Pcdhs induced cell aggregation.
source: Although all expressed δ-Pcdhs induced cell aggregation (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by aggregation assay data shown in referenced figure

claim: Pcdh10 formed very small aggregates relative to the other δ-Pcdhs.
source: Pcdh10 formed very small aggregates relative to the others.
evidence: Supported by aggregation assay data comparing aggregate sizes

claim: Varying the amount of Pcdh10 DNA had little impact on aggregate size.
source: However, varying the amount of Pcdh10 DNA had little impact on aggregate size.
evidence: Supported by DNA titration experiments shown in Figure 2B

claim: Cells expressing the same δ-Pcdh intermix while cells expressing different δ-Pcdhs segregate from one another.
source: We found that cells expressing the same δ-Pcdh intermix (Figure 2C, center diagonal) while cells expressing different δ-Pcdhs segregate from one another.
evidence: Supported by pair-wise coaggregation assay data shown in referenced figure

claim: δ-Pcdh adhesion is strictly homophilic.
source: We interpret these results to indicate that δ-Pcdh adhesion is strictly homophilic.
evidence: Inferred from pair-wise coaggregation assay results showing segregation between different δ-Pcdhs

claim: Identical results for homophilic adhesion were found for the cPcdh subfamily using the same assay.
source: Identical results were found for the cPcdh subfamily using the same assay (Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study using the same assay on cPcdhs

claim: A single mismatch causes one cPcdh population to segregate from the other, even when several cPcdhs are expressed in common.
source: Prior studies on cPcdhs using this approach showed that a single mismatch causes one population to segregate from the other, even when several cPcdhs are expressed in common (Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on cPcdh mismatch behavior

claim: 42 possible mismatch pairs of δ-Pcdhs were screened.
source: To systematically define how mismatched δ-Pcdhs influence adhesive outcomes, we screened 42 possible mismatch pairs.
evidence: Explicit statement of the number of pairs tested in the screen

claim: Mismatch coaggregation outcomes could be grouped into three broad categories: intermixing, interfacing, and segregation.
source: We discovered a range of outcomes that could be grouped into three broad categories (Figure 3A–D). In the first, the two populations intermixed (Figure 3A,B). In the second, the populations interfaced (Figure 3C), and in the last, the populations segregated from one another (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data shown in referenced figures

claim: Interfacing and intermixing behaviors exist on a continuum.
source: We also noticed that interfacing and intermixing behaviors were not binary, but instead appeared to exist on a continuum.
evidence: Inferred from observation of gradual differences in coaggregation behavior across experiments

claim: CoAg values below 0.1 indicate segregation.
source: In general, CoAg values below 0.1 indicate segregation
evidence: Based on analysis of coaggregation assay data using the CoAg index metric

claim: CoAg values between 0.1–0.2 are typical of populations that interface.
source: whereas values between 0.1–0.2 are typical of populations that interface.
evidence: Based on analysis of coaggregation assay data using the CoAg index metric

claim: CoAg values above 0.2 indicate increasingly higher degrees of intermixing.
source: Above 0.2, aggregates display increasingly higher degrees of intermixing.
evidence: Based on analysis of coaggregation assay data using the CoAg index metric

claim: Different δ-Pcdh combinations produced different coaggregation behaviors.
source: Reordering the CoAg values into a heat map strongly argued that different δ-Pcdh combinations produced different coaggregation behaviors (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by heat map analysis of mismatch coaggregation assay data shown in referenced figure

claim: Pcdh1 cells interface with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells (CoAg = 0.11).
source: For example, we combined Pcdh1 cells with cells expressing Pcdh1+Pcdh7 or Pcdh1+Pcdh8. In the first case, cells interfaced (CoAg = 0.11; row 1, column 2)
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values

claim: Pcdh1 cells intermix with Pcdh1+Pcdh8 cells (CoAg = 0.27).
source: but in the second, they intermixed (CoAg = 0.27; row 1, column 3).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values

claim: Strong asymmetry is observed across the diagonal in the mismatch coaggregation heat map.
source: This is further reinforced by the fact that strong asymmetry is observed across the diagonal in the heat map.
evidence: Supported by analysis of heat map data showing different behaviors for reciprocal mismatch pairs

claim: Pcdh19 cells segregate from Pcdh19+Pcdh7 cells (CoAg = 0.02).
source: For example, Pcdh19 cells segregate from Pcdh19+Pcdh7 cells (CoAg = 0.02; Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values shown in referenced figure

claim: Pcdh7 cells intermix with Pcdh19+Pcdh7 cells (CoAg = 0.40).
source: However, 'across the diagonal,' Pcdh7 cells intermix with these same Pcdh19+Pcdh7 cells (CoAg = 0.40).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values

claim: Pcdh19 cells intermix with Pcdh19+Pcdh9 cells (CoAg = 0.23).
source: Similarly, Pcdh19 cells intermix with Pcdh19+Pcdh9 cells (CoAg = 0.23)
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values

claim: Pcdh9 cells segregate from Pcdh19+Pcdh9 cells (CoAg = 0.07).
source: but across the diagonal, Pcdh9 cells segregate (CoAg = 0.07).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values

claim: Coaggregation is dependent upon the identity of the mismatched δ-Pcdh.
source: These results strongly suggest that coaggregation is dependent upon the identity of the mismatched δ-Pcdh.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of asymmetric and variable coaggregation behaviors depending on which δ-Pcdhs are expressed

claim: Pcdh7 cells intermixed with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells across all time points (18, 22, 26, and 44 hr post electroporation).
source: As seen in our initial screen, Pcdh7 cells intermixed with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells across all time points
evidence: Supported by time course coaggregation assay data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: Pcdh1 cells interfaced with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells across all time points (18, 22, 26, and 44 hr post electroporation).
source: whereas Pcdh1 cells interfaced (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by time course coaggregation assay data shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh1 cells segregate from Pcdh1+Pcdh17 cells (CoAg = 0.07).
source: We repeated the assay for Pcdh1+Pcdh17, and found that Pcdh1 cells segregated (CoAg = 0.07, Figure 4D–F)
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh17 cells intermix with Pcdh1+Pcdh17 cells (CoAg = 0.42).
source: while Pcdh17 cells intermixed (CoAg = 0.42).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with quantified CoAg values

claim: Controlling for surface level is important for interpreting coaggregation behavior.
source: These results argue that controlling for surface level is important for interpreting coaggregation behavior, an aspect we explore below.
evidence: Inferred from differences in results between preliminary screen and surface expression-controlled experiments

claim: The Pcdh7+Pcdh17 pair was particularly sensitive to DNA input, as small changes could alter the result despite minor effects on surface expression.
source: However, we found that this pair was particularly sensitive to DNA input, as small changes could alter the result despite minor effects on surface expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying DNA inputs shown in referenced figure

claim: Differential adhesive behaviors were maintained as combinatorial depth increased.
source: Differential adhesive behaviors were maintained as combinatorial depth increased, with the coaggregation outcome depending on which δ-Pcdhs were present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with three δ-Pcdhs shown in referenced figure

claim: δ-Pcdh expression levels vary both within and between neurons.
source: In addition, our expression data (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G) suggest that δ-Pcdh expression levels vary both within and between neurons.
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization and NanoString data shown in referenced figures

claim: Varying the expression levels in Pcdh1 cells did not alter the coaggregation behavior category (interfacing), but did affect the degree of interfacing.
source: Mean CoAg values show varying the expression levels in Pcdh1 cells did not alter the coaggregation behavior (interfacing), but did affect the degree of interfacing.
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying Pcdh1 expression levels shown in Figure 5B,C

claim: Pcdh7 (low, medium, and high) cells all still intermixed with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells.
source: while Pcdh7 (low, medium, and high) cells all still intermixed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying Pcdh7 expression levels shown in referenced figures

claim: Differences in mismatch coaggregation among δ-Pcdhs cannot be primarily explained based on variable expression in cells expressing one δ-Pcdh.
source: Thus, differences in mismatch coaggregation among δ-Pcdhs cannot be primarily explained based on variable expression in cells expressing one δ-Pcdh.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that varying expression in single δ-Pcdh cells does not change coaggregation category

claim: Varying the ratio of expression clearly altered coaggregation outcomes in cells expressing two δ-Pcdhs.
source: We found that varying the ratio of expression clearly altered coaggregation outcomes (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying relative expression levels shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh1 cells intermix with Pcdh1High+Pcdh7Low cells, but segregate from Pcdh1Low+Pcdh7High cells.
source: For example, in Figure 5D (column 1), Pcdh1 cells intermix with Pcdh1High+Pcdh7Low cells, but segregate from Pcdh1Low+Pcdh7High cells.
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying relative expression levels shown in referenced figure

claim: Relative surface levels of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs can influence aggregation behavior, even when there are no mismatches between populations.
source: Thus, relative surface levels of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs can influence aggregation behavior, even when there are no mismatches between populations.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that varying relative expression in co-expressing cells affects coaggregation with matched populations

claim: Changing the relative ratio of expression in cells expressing two δ-Pcdhs has a much greater effect on coaggregation than varying expression in cells expressing one δ-Pcdh.
source: We conclude that changing the relative ratio of expression in cells expressing two δ-Pcdhs has a much greater effect on coaggregation than varying expression in cells expressing one δ-Pcdh.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experiments varying expression in single vs. co-expressing cells

claim: Differences in apparent adhesive affinity have been argued to mediate segregation among classical cadherins, such as N- and E-cadherin.
source: Such differences have been argued to mediate segregation among classical cadherins, such as N- and E-cadherin (Harrison et al., 2010; Katsamba et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on classical cadherin adhesive properties

claim: Pcdh7 cells maintained larger aggregates than Pcdh1 or Pcdh17 cells at all speeds.
source: However, Pcdh7 cells maintained larger aggregates than Pcdh1 or Pcdh17 cells at all speeds (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by speed aggregation assay data shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh1 and Pcdh17 cells appeared to fully dissociate by ~200 RPM, while Pcdh7 aggregates were still present even at 220 RPM.
source: Furthermore, while Pcdh1 and Pcdh17 cells appeared to fully dissociate by ~200 RPM, Pcdh7 aggregates were still present even at 220 RPM.
evidence: Supported by speed aggregation assay data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: Pcdh1 cells maintained larger aggregates than Pcdh19 cells at all speeds.
source: Similarly, we found that Pcdh1 cells maintained larger aggregates than Pcdh19 cells at all speeds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by speed aggregation assay data shown in referenced figures

claim: Higher surface levels generated larger aggregates that could better withstand increasing rotational speeds.
source: As expected, we found that higher surface levels generated larger aggregates that could better withstand increasing rotational speeds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by speed aggregation assay data with varying expression levels shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh7 cells produced larger aggregates at all speeds compared to Pcdh17 cells.
source: We also found that Pcdh7 cells produced larger aggregates at all speeds compared to Pcdh17 cells.
evidence: Supported by speed aggregation assay data comparing Pcdh7 and Pcdh17

claim: Pcdh7Low cells still maintained some aggregates even at 220 RPM.
source: Even at 220 RPM, Pcdh7Low cells still maintained some aggregates.
evidence: Supported by speed aggregation assay data with low Pcdh7 expression

claim: At 120 RPM, Pcdh7 cells still intermixed with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells, but Pcdh1 cells segregated.
source: Despite the increased speed, Pcdh7 cells still intermixed with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells. However, Pcdh1 cells now segregated (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data at increased speed shown in referenced figures

claim: Low sequence identity (~35%) is found among δ-Pcdhs in extracellular domains (EC) 1–4.
source: We found low sequence identity among δ-Pcdhs in extracellular domains (EC) 1–4 (~35%; Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by MUSCLE protein alignment analysis shown in referenced figure

claim: The adhesive interface of Pcdh19 was localized to EC1-4.
source: Prior work had shown that the adhesive interface of Pcdh19 was localized to EC1-4 (Cooper et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior structural study on Pcdh19

claim: Pcdh1Δ1-4, Pcdh7Δ1-4 and Pcdh17Δ1-4 constructs were unable to mediate adhesion, although the truncated proteins were still transported to the surface.
source: Although the truncated proteins were still transported to the surface, they were unable to mediate adhesion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by aggregation assay and western blot data shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh7 cells could no longer intermix with Pcdh1+Pcdh7Δ1-4 cells, and switched to a segregation behavior (CoAg = 0.01).
source: Pcdh7 cells could no longer intermix, and switched to a segregation behavior (CoAg = 0.01; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with EC1-4 deletion construct shown in referenced figures

claim: Pcdh1 cells switched from interfacing to intermixing with Pcdh1+Pcdh7Δ1-4 cells (CoAg = 0.25).
source: Conversely, Pcdh1 cells switched from interfacing to intermixing (CoAg = 0.25).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with EC1-4 deletion construct

claim: Pcdh7EC1-4:Pcdh1 cells intermixed with Pcdh1 cells, but segregated from Pcdh7 cells.
source: These cells now intermixed with Pcdh1 cells, but segregated from Pcdh7 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D, column 3).
evidence: Supported by mismatch coaggregation assay data with EC1-4 swap construct shown in referenced figures

claim: EC1-4 mediates adhesive specificity.
source: These results are consistent with EC1-4 mediating adhesive specificity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that deletion or swapping of EC1-4 changes coaggregation behavior

claim: The Monte Carlo simulation model correctly predicted that cells expressing identical δ-Pcdhs will intermix.
source: The model functioned most optimally in predicting cells that will intermix. For example, the model correctly predicted that cells expressing identical δ-Pcdhs will intermix.
evidence: Supported by Monte Carlo simulation results shown in Figure 6E

claim: The Monte Carlo simulation model could not precisely recapitulate conditions where mismatched cells interfaced or segregated.
source: However, the model could not precisely recapitulate conditions where mismatched cells interfaced or segregated (Figure 6E, far right column; for example mixing Pcdh1 cells with Pcdh1+Pcdh7 cells).
evidence: Supported by Monte Carlo simulation results shown in referenced figure

claim: Each additional δ-Pcdh co-expressed with Pcdh7 led to a corresponding decrease in the CoAg index.
source: We found that each additional δ-Pcdh co-expressed with Pcdh7 led to a corresponding decrease in the CoAg index (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with increasing numbers of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs shown in referenced figure

claim: Pcdh7 only cells shifted from intermixing towards interfacing as the relative proportion of Pcdh7 decreased.
source: Pcdh7 only cells shifted from intermixing towards interfacing as the relative proportion of Pcdh7 decreased.
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with increasing numbers of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs

claim: The percent of Pcdh7 with respect to total surface expression decreased from ~50% to 25%, almost perfectly mirroring the decline in CoAg index (R2 = 0.94).
source: Quantification of surface expression showed that the percent of Pcdh7 with respect to total surface expression decreased from ~50% to 25%, almost perfectly mirroring the decline in CoAg index (R2 = 0.94; Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by surface expression quantification and CoAg index analysis shown in referenced figure

claim: Increasing the number of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs shifted the behavior of Pcdh1 cells from interfacing to segregation.
source: We repeated the experiment with Pcdh1, and found a similar effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B). In this case, increasing the number of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs shifted the behavior of Pcdh1 cells from interfacing to segregation.
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with increasing numbers of co-expressed δ-Pcdhs shown in referenced figures

claim: cPcdh Pcdhb11 cells completely segregate from cells expressing δ-Pcdhs.
source: We first confirmed that cPcdh Pcdhb11 cells completely segregate from cells expressing δ-Pcdhs, demonstrating strict homophilic adhesion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data shown in referenced figure

claim: At DNA input ratios of 3:4 and 1:2 (Pcdh7:Pcdhb11), Pcdh7 cells strongly intermixed while Pcdhb11 cells segregated.

evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying Pcdh7:Pcdhb11 ratios shown in referenced figures

claim: At a DNA ratio of 1:4 (Pcdh7 ~20% of total), Pcdh7 cells still intermixed but Pcdhb11 cells could now interface.
source: However, at a DNA ratio of 1:4 (Pcdh7 ~20% of total), Pcdh7 cells still intermixed but Pcdhb11 cells could now interface.
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying Pcdh7:Pcdhb11 ratios

claim: δ-Pcdhs influence the aggregation behavior of cells expressing cPcdh Pcdhb11.
source: Thus, δ-Pcdhs influence the aggregation behavior of cells expressing this particular cPcdh.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that co-expression of Pcdh7 with Pcdhb11 affects Pcdhb11 cell coaggregation behavior

claim: Cells can vary the number of δ-Pcdhs expressed per cell to tune adhesion.
source: First, we found that cells can vary the number of δ-Pcdhs expressed per cell.
evidence: Supported by NanoString data showing 0-7 δ-Pcdhs per cell and coaggregation assays showing effects of varying numbers

claim: Individual δ-Pcdhs possess differences in apparent adhesive affinity.
source: Second, we showed that individual δ-Pcdhs possess differences in apparent adhesive affinity.

claim: Differences in apparent adhesive affinity can be modulated by varying relative surface expression levels.
source: Third, we further demonstrated that these differences can be modulated by varying relative surface expression levels.

source: These principles contrast with those defined for the cPcdhs.

claim: δ-Pcdhs can modify cPcdh adhesion.
source: Despite these differences, we show δ-Pcdhs can modify cPcdh adhesion.

claim: cPcdhs have been shown to be important for neuronal survival, dendritogenesis, synapse formation, and self-avoidance.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on cPcdh functions

claim: For the cPcdhs, the particular combination of cPcdhs expressed does not appear to be a critical factor in adhesion.

source: Despite this, such differences do not appear to have a major impact in K562 assays (Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior K562 aggregation assay study on cPcdhs

claim: In a prior cPcdh study, two populations would only fully intermix if they expressed the same combinations of cPcdhs.
source: In this paper, two populations would only fully intermix if they expressed the same combinations of cPcdhs.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior cPcdh aggregation study

claim: In a prior cPcdh study, if even one cPcdh differed between two populations, the populations would completely segregate, regardless of the identity of the mismatched cPcdh.
source: If even one cPcdh differed between the two, the populations would completely segregate, regardless of the identity of the mismatched cPcdh.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior cPcdh aggregation study

claim: The observed cPcdh results were always binary in nature, producing either complete intermixing or complete segregation.
source: The observed results were always binary in nature, and produced either complete intermixing or complete segregation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior cPcdh aggregation study

claim: δ-Pcdhs appear to use some of the same principles as classical cadherins for mediating cell sorting.
source: Thus, δ-Pcdhs appear to use some of the same principles as classical cadherins.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of δ-Pcdh results with Steinberg's differential adhesion hypothesis for classical cadherins

claim: Steinberg's differential adhesion hypothesis provides a framework for understanding how classical cadherins mediate cell sorting.
source: Steinberg's differential adhesion hypothesis provides a commonly used framework for understanding how classical cadherins mediate cell sorting.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about Steinberg's hypothesis

claim: In Steinberg's model, cells sort from one another to reach an optimal thermodynamic equilibrium, driven by differences in adhesive affinity and/or expression level.
source: In this model, cells sort from one another to reach an optimal thermodynamic equilibrium. This sorting can be driven by differences in adhesive affinity between cells, and/or by differences in expression level (Foty and Steinberg, 2005; Friedlander et al., 1989; Steinberg and Takeichi, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on Steinberg's differential adhesion hypothesis

claim: The ECTM domain mediated homophilic adhesion to a degree similar to that of the full-length construct.
source: However, we demonstrated that the ECTM domain mediated homophilic adhesion to a degree similar to that of the full-length construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by aggregation assay data comparing ECTM and full-length constructs shown in referenced figure

claim: The ECTM domain is typically used to study δ-Pcdh adhesion.
source: In addition, the ECTM domain is typically used to study δ-Pcdh adhesion (Chen et al., 2007; Cooper et al., 2016; Emond et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies using ECTM domains

claim: δ-Pcdhs can interact in cis.
source: In particular, Pederick et al. showed δ-Pcdhs can interact in cis (Pederick et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study demonstrating cis interactions

claim: Cis interactions have been proposed to be critical for cPcdh function.
source: Such cis interactions have previously been proposed to be critical for cPcdh function (Rubinstein et al., 2017; Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on cPcdh cis interactions

claim: δ-Pcdhs have been suspected to be expressed in combination in vivo based on double-label RNA in situ data.
source: First, while δ-Pcdhs have been suspected to be expressed in combination in vivo based on double-label RNA in situ data, there has been no prior evidence demonstrating the extent of this expression.
evidence: Inferred from prior literature and the novelty of the current study's findings

claim: The combinatorial expression of δ-Pcdhs is not an entirely random event, as has been suggested for the cPcdhs.
source: Thus, the combinatorial expression of δ-Pcdhs is not an entirely random event, as has been suggested for the cPcdhs (Goodman et al., 2016; Hirano et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from spatially restricted expression patterns and differential co-expression with odorant receptors, contrasted with cited cPcdh studies

claim: Mis- and over-expression of Pcdh10 in the olfactory system caused defects in glomerular target formation by OSNs expressing the Olfr9 odorant receptor, but not by those expressing Olfr17.
source: For example, we previously showed that mis- and over-expression of Pcdh10 in the olfactory system caused defects in glomerular target formation by OSNs expressing the Olfr9 odorant receptor, but not by those expressing Olfr17 (Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on Pcdh10 function in OSN targeting

claim: A recently generated Pcdh19 mutant mouse shows targeting defects of a subset of OSN populations.
source: A recently generated Pcdh19 mutant mouse in our lab also shows targeting defects of a subset of OSN populations (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by unpublished data from the authors' lab

claim: Loss of any one δ-Pcdh would alter the combination of δ-Pcdhs expressed and change the relative expression of co-expressed protocadherins.
source: Loss of any one δ-Pcdh would alter the combination of δ-Pcdhs expressed and change the relative expression of co-expressed protocadherins.
evidence: Inferred from the principles established in the study about how combinations and relative expression affect adhesion

claim: Single cell RNA-seq studies have been unable to adequately address what combinations of δ-Pcdhs are expressed within individual neurons.
source: However, defining the particular combination of δ-Pcdhs expressed per neuron has been problematic. Single cell RNA-seq studies have been unable to adequately address what combinations are expressed within individual neurons.
evidence: Supported by comparison of NanoString data with three single cell RNA-seq datasets showing lower detection in RNA-seq

claim: Three single OSN RNA-seq datasets show an average detection of ~1 δ-Pcdh per neuron, while the NanoString approach detects ~3.5.
source: Our own analysis of three single OSN RNA-seq datasets (Hanchate et al., 2015; Saraiva et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2015) shows an average detection of ~1 δ-Pcdh per neuron, while our NanoString approach detects ~3.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K,L).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of NanoString and RNA-seq data shown in referenced figures

claim: Co-expression of Pcdh7 with Pcdhb11 inhibits Pcdhb11 from intermixing with Pcdh7+Pcdhb11 cells.
source: We demonstrated co-expression of Pcdh7 with Pcdhb11 inhibits Pcdhb11 from intermixing with Pcdh7+Pcdhb11 cells (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data shown in referenced figures

claim: If expression of Pcdh7 is reduced relative to Pcdhb11, then Pcdhb11 cells begin to display interfacing behavior.
source: If, however, expression of Pcdh7 is reduced relative to Pcdhb11, then these cells begin to display interfacing behavior.
evidence: Supported by coaggregation assay data with varying Pcdh7:Pcdhb11 ratios

claim: δ-Pcdhs, classical cadherins, cPcdhs, and other subfamily members are all likely to be co-expressed within individual neurons.
source: It seems reasonable that δ-Pcdhs, classical cadherins, cPcdhs, and other subfamily members are all likely to be co-expressed within individual neurons.
evidence: Speculative statement based on known expression patterns and the demonstration of interfamily interactions

claim: δ-Pcdhs can bind and regulate classical cadherins.
source: For example, δ-Pcdhs can bind and regulate classical cadherins (Chen and Gumbiner, 2006; Chen et al., 2009; Emond et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on δ-Pcdh interactions with classical cadherins

claim: Deletion of cPcdhs leads to neuronal death and to defects in dendritic self-avoidance in the retina.
source: In the retina, deletion of cPcdhs leads to neuronal death and to defects in dendritic self-avoidance.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of cPcdh functions in the retina

claim: Interactions between cPcdh subfamilies accentuates effects on neuronal death and dendritic self-avoidance in the retina.
source: Interestingly, interactions between cPcdh subfamilies accentuates these effects (Ing-Esteves et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on cPcdh subfamily interactions

claim: In the cortex, deletion of cPcdhs disrupts dendritic branching due to a failure to promote arborization.
source: However, in the cortex, deletion of cPcdhs disrupts dendritic branching due to a failure to promote arborization (Molumby et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on cPcdh functions in the cortex

claim: The same cPcdh family has distinct effects in different regions of the nervous system.
source: Thus, the same family has distinct effects in different regions of the nervous system.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cPcdh effects in retina vs. cortex

claim: These regional differences in cPcdh effects were proposed to be due to context dependent effects.
source: These differences were proposed to be due to context dependent effects.
evidence: Supported by prior literature on cPcdh functions

claim: Interfamily interactions, such as those between the δ-Pcdhs and the cPcdhs, may play a role in explaining varying cPcdh phenotypes.
source: However, it is conceivable that interfamily interactions, such as those between the δ-Pcdhs and the cPcdhs, may also play a role in explaining these varying phenotypes.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the demonstration of δ-Pcdh/cPcdh interactions in this study
